16770-the-adventure-of-two-dutch-dolls-a:
Bertha Upton wrote the words and Florence K. Upton drew the pictures for this early picture book, issued by DeWolfe, Fiske in Boston. It opens on a frosty Christmas Eve. Peggy Deutchland wakes from wooden sleep on a shop counter. She calls her neighbor Sarah Jane to rise at midnight, when dolls and toys taste human joys. The pair long to try their limbs and dance a jig.

The book mixes verse and pictures, as the dolls meet a little girl and a golliwog toy on their night adventure. Its charm lies in toy life after dark, told in short, singable lines. Modern readers should note its period character types with care, while young readers of its day loved it as a Christmas toy tale.
britannica-1911-brigg:
Brigg, properly Glanford Brigg or Glamford Bridge, is a market town in Lincolnshire, England, on the river Ancholme, which gives water passage to the Humber. The urban district held 3137 people in 1901. It stands 23 miles by road north of Lincoln and is served by the Grimsby line of the Great Central railway.

Trade is chiefly farming, as befits a market town in corn country. Antiquity gives the entry its striking find: in 1885 a remarkable boat, judged early British work, was dug up near the river. Hollowed from a single oak trunk, it measures 48 feet 6 inches long by about 5 feet wide. Other remains from before written history have also turned up nearby, tying the modern market town to very old settlement by the Ancholme.
podcast-dannyjones--YF-U2uk4Gg:
Retired Navy admiral Tim Gallaudet brings an unusual resume to Danny Jones's podcast: oceanographer, former head of a federal science agency, and a public voice on unidentified objects in the sea. Gallaudet warns that unknown objects are shadowing American nuclear submarines, and he treats the reports as a safety and security problem.

Much of the talk centers on what sailors and sensors have recorded under water, where objects reportedly move in ways no known craft can match. Gallaudet argues the Navy knows more than it releases and should study the sightings openly. Whether listeners accept his reading or not, hearing a flag officer make the case in plain terms is the episode's draw.
podcast-dannyjones-1osA51kvzgg:
Dan Richards returns to Danny Jones's podcast for a conversation that jumps between three loaded subjects. They are the Jeffrey Epstein case, the legend of Atlantis, and the Ark of the Covenant from the Hebrew Bible. Richards links scandal, lost civilization, and sacred relic hunting into one wide-ranging discussion.

Jones lets the topics collide rather than keeping them in separate lanes, which is the show's style at its loosest. Epstein brings the modern true-crime thread, Atlantis the ancient-mystery thread, and the Ark the biblical one. None of the claims is settled here, and the recording is preserved as the conversation happened. Listeners who enjoy speculative history mixed with current scandal will get exactly that mixture.
podcast-tuckercarlson-3fikmsCkjgg:
Reporter Catherine Herridge speaks with Tucker Carlson about court pressure, firing, and big stories. Herridge had covered national security for major networks. She faced a court fight over a source she would not name.

She recalls her son asking if she might go to jail. She links her firing to work on the Hunter Biden laptop story. The pair also discuss the Trump and Biden debate and how Biden had changed. The episode frames her case as a test of press freedom in a hard election season. Her calm tone makes the stakes feel even higher.
the-adventure-of-two-dutch-dolls-and-a-g:
Bertha Upton wrote the words and Florence K. Upton drew the pictures for The Adventures of Two Dutch Dolls and a Golliwogg, printed at Boston by DeWolfe, Fiske and Co. The tale is told in light verse with a picture on near each page.

On a frosty Christmas Eve, Peggy Deutchland wakes from her wooden sleep on a shop counter and calls to her neighbor Sarah Jane. Midnight, she says, is the hour when toys wake and take their fun. She longs to stretch her wooden limbs and dance a jig after twelve long months shut in. Readers meet the pair's night of fun with the Golliwogg, in the book that first brought that figure to fame.
